analysis.one_liner: Cuts PAC contribution limits, bans soft money and bundled donations, and requires lobbyist and union political-spending disclosure.
analysis.headline: A Republican-led campaign finance bill that would have cut PAC contribution limits by 80 percent and banned soft money was referred to three House committees and never received a hearing, a vote, or floor action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have cut the most a political action committee can give a candidate from $5,000 to $1,000 per election, banned the unlimited 'soft money' donations party committees used to bankroll federal campaigns, barred PAC-to-PAC contributions and bundled giving, and required lobbyists to disclose their donations. It also would have capped out-of-state money at 49 percent of a House candidate's total, required labor unions to tell members annually how their dues are spent on politics and reduce dues by that amount, stripped tax-exempt status from politically active nonprofits, and doubled the total one individual could give each year from $25,000 to $50,000. It died without a vote when the 103rd Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters who want House elections funded mainly by people in the district rather than by PACs and national soft money; challengers running against incumbents backed by PAC money; employees who would learn annually how much of their dues funds political activity and could reduce dues accordingly; and donors who want to see when lobbyists give.

how_it_helps.text: Cuts the maximum contribution a multicandidate PAC can give a federal candidate from $5,000 to $1,000 per election, shrinking the weight of organized industry and union money in House races.

Bans 'soft money' — money raised outside federal limits and disclosure rules that party committees used to influence federal elections — and limits what state and local party committees can accept for federal-influencing activity.
Prohibits contributions made through intermediaries or conduits (bundling) and bans PAC-to-PAC contributions, closing channels that obscure who is really behind a check.
Requires lobbyists to attach a written statement of their lobbyist status to any contribution and to report contributions to the FEC within 20 days of month's end.
Caps out-of-State contributions at 49 percent of a House candidate's total contributions and requires campaigns to itemize them, aimed at keeping representatives dependent on home-district donors.

Requires labor unions to notify all bargaining-unit employees annually that no one can be forced to fund the union's political activities, and to reduce dues by each member's share of political spending, with independent CPA verification and an impartial process for challenges.
Lengthens from 60 to 90 days the pre-election period during which Members of Congress may not send franked mass mailings at taxpayer expense.

analysis.who_pays: Political action committees of every kind, whose giving power would drop by 80 percent; political party committees, which would lose soft money and face new accounting and disclosure rules for federal-influencing activity; labor unions, which would bear new notice, audit, and escrow obligations and lose the ability to use dues for politics without member notice; and tax-exempt groups, which would lose their exemption if any of their budget goes to voter registration or election activity.

drawbacks.text: The bill doubles the aggregate amount one individual may give each year from $25,000 to $50,000, handing the biggest donors more room while cutting everyone else's channels of influence.

It denies tax-exempt status to any organization that devotes any of its budget to voter registration, get-out-the-vote drives, or campaign activity, which would strip tax exemption from a wide range of civic and advocacy groups that conduct registration drives, not just campaign arms.
The 49 percent out-of-state cap can fall hardest on challengers and candidates from small states, who often must raise money beyond their district to compete with incumbents' networks.

The union provisions were certain to draw a constitutional and political fight: supporters framed them as protecting employees from compelled political payments, while union opponents would argue they hobble organized labor's ability to speak in elections relative to corporations, whose political activity faces no comparable notice regime in the bill.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core of the bill — an 80 percent cut in PAC contribution limits, a soft-money ban, a bundling ban, and lobbyist disclosure — targets the channels through which organized money influences House elections, and it would have delivered real transparency and limits. It is not clean: it doubles the ceiling for the biggest individual donors, and its tax-exemption provision is so broad it would hit charities conducting voter registration drives rather than just campaign vehicles. The union disclosure and dues provisions are defensible on their face — employees should know what their dues fund — but they apply pressure to only one side of the organized-money ledger. On balance a genuine reform bill with real drafting flaws, and it never got close to a vote.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to three House committees the day it was introduced; none of them ever acted on it, and it expired when the 103rd Congress ended in January 1995 without a hearing or vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Tillie Fowler of Florida and 20 Republican cosponsors introduced the bill on September 30, 1993.
The same day, it was referred to the House Committees on House Administration, Ways and Means, and Post Office and Civil Service.
No further action of any kind — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor vote — is recorded for the remainder of the Congress.
The Congress ended on January 3, 1995, killing the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: PACs, party committees that relied on soft money, and incumbent officeholders who benefit from the existing flow of large and undisclosed checks are better off, because the limits and disclosure rules the bill would have imposed never became law.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 20 cosponsors were Republicans, with no Democratic cosponsors, and the bill received no action in committees controlled by the Democratic majority.

industries.industry: Political action committees (corporate, trade, and union PACs)
industries.note: The bill cuts PAC contribution limits from $5,000 to $1,000 per election, bans PAC-to-PAC giving, and requires PACs to carry their sponsoring organization's full name. PAC money is the primary channel by which organized industry and labor buy access to House members, so the reduction would directly shrink that influence.

The bill bans soft money — unlimited, largely unreported money that party committees raised to influence federal elections — and imposes allocation and disclosure rules on party accounts and state and local party federal activity. Parties would lose their least-regulated funding channel.

Unions face new annual notice, dues-reduction, CPA audit, and escrow requirements tied to political spending, and the PAC cut hits union PACs like anyone else's. But the same provisions guarantee employees are never forced to fund union politics and give them an audited, contestable accounting — a real benefit to the workers themselves.

Any tax-exempt organization spending any part of its budget on voter registration, get-out-the-vote, or federal campaign activity would lose tax exemption, and groups whose solicitations a candidate cooperates in would lose it as well. This sweeps in nonpartisan civic groups along with campaign-front organizations.
While restricting every other channel, the bill doubles the aggregate amount one person can give each year from $25,000 to $50,000, increasing the relative weight of the wealthiest donors.
